target: AG1's claim that AI is broadly good for society because it improves convenience, health, accessibility, safety, productivity, and learning
objection: AI's apparent benefits are outweighed by major harms: it can displace workers and depress wages, weaken critical thinking through overreliance, reproduce and amplify racial bias, create large privacy risks through data collection, and expand workplace surveillance.

target: AG2's claim that AI's harms make it harmful overall
objection: AG2 treats AI's harms as inevitabilities, but AG1 argues they are engineering and policy problems that can be mitigated through governance, design, fairness audits, privacy-preserving methods, and human oversight, so they do not prove AI is inherently harmful.

Even if safeguards exist in theory, incentives to collect data and deploy quickly, weak enforcement, and competitive pressures make responsible governance unreliable in practice, so mitigation does not justify calling AI socially good overall.

target: AG2's claim that safeguards are unreliable and therefore AI cannot be net good
objection: AI can still be socially beneficial if enforceable rules, audits, transparency, liability, and worker protections are put in place; AG2 has shown that risk management is necessary, not that AI cannot be deployed in ways that produce net benefits.

target: AG1's claim that enforceable governance and policy can make AI socially beneficial
objection: Enforcement is structurally hard because regulators lack technical capacity and real-time access, harms are externalized onto individuals who must prove and remedy them, and AI tends to concentrate power in large firms, so the governance fixes AG1 proposes are not enough to make AI good overall.

target: AG2's argument that enforcement limits, externalized harms, and power concentration defeat the case for AI
objection: Those are implementation problems, not reasons to reject AI: liability, audit logs, remedies, transparency, interoperability, and competition policy can reduce externalities and concentration, preserving AI's net societal benefits.

target: AG1's claim that liability, audits, remedies, and policy can solve the enforcement and concentration problems
objection: Meaningful verification is blocked by proprietary opacity and information asymmetry, many AI harms are subtle or hard to reverse, and competition plus data/compute advantages still push power toward dominant firms, so the governance tools AG1 cites do not reliably prevent harm.

target: AG2's claim that opacity, hard-to-detect harms, and concentration prevent AI from being net good
objection: AI does not need perfect oversight everywhere to be socially beneficial; by focusing on lower-risk, high-benefit uses and applying selective deployment, human-in-the-loop controls, and impact monitoring, society can capture benefits while managing the riskiest cases.

target: AG1's selective deployment and risk-tiering approach
objection: Even low-risk AI uses still create privacy and bias harms at scale, benign systems often undergo scope creep into higher-risk uses, and human-in-the-loop controls do not prevent users from outsourcing thinking or being affected by subtle harms.

target: AG2's claim that selective deployment fails because of scope creep and residual harms
objection: Scope creep and reliance failures can be reduced with technical and contractual deployment controls, hard use-case gates, sandboxing, audit trails, and interaction design that forces verification, so the existence of risk does not prove AI is net harmful.

target: AG1's claim that deployment gates, licensing, and verification prompts can control AI risks
objection: Those controls break down as models drift and are updated, downstream misuse is difficult to track across products and workflows, and verification prompts do not restore genuine critical thinking for most users, leaving the same harms in place.

target: AG2's claim that drift, misuse, and weak user verification defeat selective deployment
objection: Lifecycle governance can handle drift through versioning, staged rollouts, regression testing, and rollback; technical deployment controls can limit misuse; and thinking scaffolds can reduce cognitive offloading, so AI can still be net good overall.

target: AG1's lifecycle governance and technical-control defense
objection: Rollback cannot undo already-occurring privacy leaks or biased decisions, compliance burdens favor large firms and thereby concentrate power, and thinking scaffolds still do not overcome user time pressure or inability to properly evaluate outputs, so these mitigations do not establish a net-good case.

target: AG2's claim that even lifecycle controls and scaffolds fail to make AI good for society
objection: Net good does not require perfect undoing of harms; society can accept regulated technologies when expected outcomes improve. Baseline standards, public audits, liability, and targeted deployment can make AI beneficial, especially for accessibility, health support, and safer workflows.
